claims.text: AlCoFeNi is a high-entropy alloy that exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature.
Co can be partially replaced by Cr to form AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi while leaving the nominal amounts of Al, Fe, and Ni unchanged.
Co is ferromagnetic and Cr is antiferromagnetic in the rationale for this substitution.
Replacing part of Co with Cr in AlCoFeNi increases coercivity.
Lower annealing temperatures promote decomposition into an ordered B2 and disordered BCC two-phase mixture.
Room-temperature magnetic hysteresis measurements provide a robust evaluation of the proposed coercivity effect.
Cr substitution and annealing produce a heterogeneous microstructure containing nanoscale regions and interfaces.
The heterogeneous regions correspond to distinct ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases.
Interfaces between the proposed ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Replacement of Co by Cr substantially reduces the saturation magnetization of AlCoFeNi.
Cr substitution reduces saturation magnetization locally within the heterogeneous microstructure.
Cr substitution fosters exchange pinning at phase interfaces.
Exchange and domain-wall pinning increase resistance to domain-wall motion and thereby increase coercivity.
AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi will have a higher coercive field than matched unmodified AlCoFeNi.
The microstructural decomposition length scale depends on Cr content and annealing temperature.
If the desired two-phase microstructure does not develop, the coercivity enhancement may be reduced or absent.

contradictions.description: The boundary and uncertainty fields state that failure to obtain the two-phase microstructure may merely indicate that the processing window was missed and that coercivity enhancement may consequently be absent. The falsification rule nevertheless treats non-observation of that microstructure, or lack of coercivity increase without requiring verified attainment of the stated conditions, as falsifying the hypothesis.
